_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Mathematics unit lecture film, Time and Direction. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own steps in order (Telling the time; How long did it take?; Which unit of time?; Reading a timetable and Which bus do you catch?; North, south, east, west; Find your way), and every number in it is the lesson's own: the hour hand crept halfway to 4 at half past three (the lesson's How do you know? bank), 10:40 to 11:15 is 35 minutes counted on through 11:00 (the same bank), 2 weeks is 14 days (the interval chapter's own days-in-weeks bank, round14long kind 0, w = rnd(2, 8) so w = 2 is inside range and 2 x 7 = 14), Amina walking to school in about 15 minutes (Which unit of time?), Hodan needing the Library by 10:00 with Bus 3 at 10:10 and Bus 2 at 9:45 (Which bus do you catch?), and Home to School on the map as 2 squares east then 2 squares north (Find your way).
title: Time and Direction
subtitle: Grade 3 Mathematics
objectives: Choose the appropriate unit of time for familiar activities.
Read and record time accurately in digital notation (12-hour) and on analogue clocks.
Interpret and use the information in timetables (12-hour clock).
Understand the difference between a time and a time interval. Find time intervals between the same units in days, weeks, months and years.
Interpret and create descriptions of position, direction and movement, including reference to cardinal points.

beats.say: A clock tells you when. A compass tells you which way.
Today you will use both, and work out how long things take.
A clock has two hands, and they do different jobs.
The long hand gives the minutes. Each number it passes is five minutes.
The short hand gives the hour. Read the number it has just passed.
The long hand is at 3, and the short hand has passed 3. Quarter past three.
Now the long hand moves to 6. Half past three, and the short hand has crept halfway to 4.
A time is a point in the day. A time interval is how long something lasts.
A film starts at 10:40 and ends at 11:15. How long is it?
Do not take one time from the other. An hour is sixty minutes, not a hundred.
Count on instead. 10:40 to 11:00 is twenty minutes.
Then 11:00 to 11:15 is fifteen more. Twenty and fifteen make 35 minutes.
It works for weeks too. 2 weeks is 7 days, then 7 more: 14 days.
Some things take seconds. Others take minutes, hours, days or years.
Amina walks to school. Is that 15 seconds, 15 minutes or 15 hours?
15 seconds is far too quick. You would not reach the gate.
15 hours is far too long. That is most of a day.
15 minutes fits. Picture the thing happening, then choose the unit.
A timetable sets out times in rows and columns.
Each column is one bus. Each row is one stop.
Hodan must be at the Library by 10 o'clock. Which bus?
Find the Library row, and keep a finger on it. Bus 3 arrives at 10:10, too late.
Bus 2 arrives at 9:45, so Hodan catches Bus 2.
North, south, east and west are the four cardinal points.
On a map, north is up and south is down.
East is to the right, and west is to the left.
Your left and right change when you turn. North never does.
Clockwise is the way a clock's hands go. Anticlockwise is the other way.
Here is a map. Amina starts at the Home.
Go 2 squares east, which is 2 squares to the right.
Then go 2 squares north, which is 2 squares up the map.
Amina reaches the School. Say those words and anyone can follow them.
Face west, turn a quarter turn clockwise, and you face north.
The short hand gives the hour, and the long hand gives the minutes.
Count on to find how long, and choose a unit that fits.
Read a timetable by row and column. North, south, east and west never move.
